stops.name: The sickbed camp, news of the death of Jochi
stops.campa: Word reaches the sickbed that Jochi, the eldest son whose paternity the camp has half-doubted ever since the Merkit captivity, has died in his own territory on the Syr Darya: of illness, the messengers say, though the khan had lately summoned him to account for staying away from every campaign of the last years and had begun to suspect open defiance. Grief and old suspicion tangle in the same breath; the punitive column already gathered against his own son is stood down unused, and the succession question that will trouble every khanate after him narrows by one name no one living can now ask forgiveness of.

stops.name: Liupanshan, the death of the khan
stops.campa: In the cool of the Liupan mountains, south of the Tangut capital he will not live to see fall, the fever from his fall the winter before finally overcomes him. He leaves his sons a last counsel on unbroken unity and on the joy a man may take, even at the end, in the defeat of his enemies, and dictates the plan, carried out seven years later to the letter, for finishing the Jin by passing an army through Song territory to strike Kaifeng from its unguarded south. He dies on the eighteenth of August in his sixty-fifth year, ruler of more earth than any man before him.
stops.quote: The greatest joy for a man is to defeat his enemies, to drive them before him, to take all they possess, to see those they love in tears, to ride their horses, and to hold their wives and daughters in his arms.
stops.quote_source: Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), Chinggis Khan's reply to his generals on man's greatest joy

stops.name: Zhongxing: the order kept, the Tangut ended
stops.campa: Obeying the order given while he still lived, his sons complete the siege in secret. The Tangut emperor Mozhu, unaware that the khan he is surrendering to has already been six weeks dead, is brought out with the keys of Zhongxing and executed on the spot despite the terms he was offered; the city is given over to slaughter and plunder so thorough it all but erases the Tangut state from the map. Not a word of the khan's own death is allowed to leave the army; any traveler who crosses the path of what is coming is killed to keep the secret, exactly as the dying order required.

stops.name: The secret cortège, home to Burkhan Khaldun
stops.campa: For weeks the cortège crosses the width of the Gobi with the khan's body under close guard, killing every herder and traveler it meets on the road so that no rumor can outrun it home. A thousand horses are driven back and forth over the fresh-dug grave until no mark of digging remains, and a diverted stream is let run across it so that even the escort could not return to point out the place. He is carried at last to the mountain that once sheltered a frightened young man fleeing the Merkits, and buried there without mound, marker, or monument, among the trees of his own vow.

stops.name: Burkhan Khaldun: the Ikh Khorig, the forbidden zone, still unfound
stops.campa: His successors set a thousand household guardsmen, the Uriankhai keshig, to seal the mountain and its valleys as the Ikh Khorig, the Great Taboo, forbidden to any foot but their own. For seven centuries the ban holds, under Yuan, under Qing, even under a Soviet-era Mongolia that kept the whole province closed as a restricted military zone. No expedition, Mongolian or foreign, ground search or satellite survey, has yet named the grave with certainty, and Mongolian law and custom alike still ask that none should try. The mountain keeps the vow he made to it, and the vow he asked back from it, in the same unbroken silence.
